summary: This informational document looks at the fixed 64-bit boundary in IPv6 unicast addresses, where the first part identifies the subnet and the last part identifies the interface. It describes the advantages of keeping the boundary fixed and examines the issues that would arise if it were made variable.

plainLanguage.summary: An IPv6 address has two halves: a prefix that says which subnet the address is on, and an interface identifier that says which device on that subnet owns it. The rules fix the second half at 64 bits, so every subnet is a /64. RFC 7421 explains where that number came from, what it makes simpler, and what would break if a shorter identifier and a longer prefix were allowed.

questions: can i use a prefix longer than /64
why is an ipv6 subnet 64 bits
where does the 64 bit boundary come from
subtitle: Why an IPv6 subnet is always 64 bits long, and what would break if that boundary could move.

tldr.problem: An IPv6 address is split into a subnet prefix and an interface identifier, and the rules fix the identifier at 64 bits, which fixes every subnet at a /64. People keep asking why the boundary cannot simply move.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7421 traces where the 64 came from, lists what a fixed length buys, sets out the arguments for changing it, and then works through the specifications, protocols and implementations that would have to change, including measurements of how current systems behave with other prefix lengths.
tldr.outcome: The document makes no proposal. It records that the consensus in the IETF is that the benefits of the fixed length and the difficulty of changing it outweigh the arguments for change.

today: RFC 7421 is an Informational RFC published in January 2015, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. It is an analysis that makes no proposal: it records the arguments on both sides and the consensus that the fixed length should stay.

sections.title: Where the 64 Came From
sections.content:
IPv6 addresses were made 128 bits long to give flexibility and new possibilities, rather than merely to double the size of the IPv4 address. One of those possibilities was a well-defined interface identifier: the addressing architecture divides a unicast address into n bits of subnet prefix followed by 128 minus n bits of interface identifier, the identifier is opaque once it has been derived, and because routing is entirely based on variable length prefixes, nothing in the architecture requires n to have any fixed value. All IPv6 routing protocols support prefixes of any length up to /128.

The length of the identifier is nevertheless a parameter in stateless address autoconfiguration, and it is set in a separate document for each link type. The autoconfiguration protocol itself does not define the length, and DHCPv6 does not include a prefix length in its address assignment. The /64 boundary was introduced after the initial design, in a period when /80 had been expected, for two reasons. The first was the original 8+8 proposal, which eventually led to the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol and required a fixed point for the split between the local and the wide-area part of the address. The second was the expectation that 64-bit Extended Unique Identifier MAC addresses would become widespread in place of 48-bit ones, together with the plan at the time that auto-configured addresses would be derived from those MAC addresses. The addressing architecture does describe how to form identifiers from IEEE EUI-64 hardware addresses, which fixes them at 64 bits, and the architecture as modified now requires interface identifiers to be 64 bits long.

In practice, almost every interface identifier in use is 64 bits. The only documented exception is a specification that standardises 127-bit prefixes for point-to-point links between routers, among other things, to avoid a loop condition known as the ping-pong problem. Apart from that exception, using a shorter identifier with a longer prefix is outside the current specifications, so results may vary.
sections.plainLanguage: When IPv6 was designed, the split between the subnet part of an address and the device part was expected to sit at 80 bits. It ended up at 64 for two reasons: one proposal needed a fixed point for the split, and the plan at the time was that every device would build its address from the MAC address in its hardware, which is 64 bits wide. Everything since then has been built on that number.

sections.title: What a Fixed Length Buys
sections.content:
The existence of an identifier of a given length is a necessary part of stateless address autoconfiguration, and the length is normally the same for all nodes on a given link that uses it. Although the length is a parameter set separately for each link type, a single global length for all media is the simplest solution and matches the principles of Internet host configuration.

An identifier of significant length, clearly separated from the prefix, makes it possible to limit how traceable a host is by varying the identifier. It also guarantees that there are always enough addresses in any subnet to add one or more real or virtual interfaces; there may be other limits, but IP addressing will never get in the way.

Fixing the identifier at 64 bits fixes the subnet prefix at 64 bits too, whatever aggregate prefix the site has been given, which in accordance with the address assignment policy for end sites should be a /56 or shorter. The document lists what that buys. Everything is the same: compared with IPv4 there is no more calculating leaf subnet sizes, no more juggling between subnets and fewer consequent errors, so network design is simpler and more straightforward, for every kind of network and every kind of operator. Adding a subnet is easy, because taking another /64 from the pool needs no estimate, calculation or judgement. Router configurations are homogeneous and easier to understand. Documentation is easier to write and easier to read, and training is easier.

The document records that the consensus in the IETF is that the benefits of keeping the length fixed at 64 bits, and the practical difficulties of changing it, outweigh the arguments for change.
sections.plainLanguage: A fixed 64-bit split makes three things easier. Every subnet is the same size, so there is nothing to calculate and nothing to get wrong. Adding a subnet means taking the next block of addresses from the pool. And because the identifier is separate from the prefix, a device can change its identifier and be harder to track. The IETF's view is that these benefits, plus the cost of changing, settle the question.

sections.title: The Arguments for Something Else
sections.content:
Several arguments have been made for shorter identifiers, which would allow longer prefixes. The first is insufficient address space: a site may be delegated a prefix too small to give a /64 to each of its internal subnets, and may then use internal prefixes longer than /64 with manually configured addresses or DHCPv6. The scenarios suggested for this are home and small office networks, vehicles, building services and transportation services such as road signs. The home network architecture text says that customer premises equipment should treat a lack of sufficient address space as an error condition rather than use prefixes longer than /64 internally. The document also rejects the idea that address registries are running out of prefix space: the released unicast space, 2000::/3, contains 35 trillion /48 prefixes, of which only a small fraction have been allocated, allowing for a conservative estimate of allocation efficiency approximately 5 trillion /48 prefixes can be allocated, and even with a relaxed estimate approximately one trillion can be allocated, and about 85 percent of the space is still in reserve.

The second argument is hierarchical addressing: some operators want more prefix bits for an aggregated hierarchy inside a campus or corporate network. But a site given a /48 already has 16 bits for hierarchical allocation, and flat interior gateway protocol routing is widely and successfully used within networks with hundreds of routers and thousands of end systems, so there is no objective need for more prefix bits.

The third is auditing: some operators want to know and audit the nodes active on a network, especially those allowed to communicate off-link, and want to limit the number of addresses and sessions sourced from a host or site. Using long prefixes with few possible hosts would make this easier, but such sites typically use DHCPv6, which means the servers already know every legitimate host, and those hosts could be limited to a small range of identifier values without changing the /64 length. Hosts that pick up addresses by autoconfiguration can be audited from neighbour discovery logs.

The fourth is neighbour discovery cache exhaustion, where an attacker floods a subnet with requests to inactive addresses to fill a router's cache and deny service to the active devices. Using a /120 prefix would limit the addresses in the subnet to something like an IPv4 /24, but the prefix has to be very long for that to work, because the number of possible cache slots has to be of the same order as the number of hosts: even 2^32 potential entries, a factor of two billion fewer than 2^64, is still more than enough to exhaust the memory of current routers. Several other mitigations are described elsewhere, and a /127 prefix already solves the case of a point-to-point link.
sections.plainLanguage: The usual reasons for wanting a different split all have answers in the document. A site short of address space should be given more by its provider, because the pool of prefixes is nowhere near exhausted. A large company does not need more bits for hierarchy, because a /48 already gives it 16. A site that wants to know and limit its hosts can use DHCPv6 and the neighbour discovery logs. And shrinking the subnet to protect a router's neighbour cache would have to shrink so far that it would not help.

sections.title: What Changing the Length Would Break
sections.content:
The 64-bit length is mentioned in many specifications, and it is not straightforward to separate the cases where it matters from those where it does not, but all of those documents would need updating, which would take considerable time and effort. The architectural documents state or repeat the value outright: the addressing architecture, the address assignment policy for end sites, the specification of reserved identifiers and the ILNP node identifiers, and customer edge routers impose /64 on their interfaces. Numerous documents that carry IPv6 over a particular kind of link make mandatory statements about the length of the identifier to use during autoconfiguration, covering Ethernet, FDDI, Token Ring, ATM, ARCnet, Frame Relay, IEEE 1394, Fibre Channel, IEEE 802.15.4, PPP, IEEE 802.16, 6over4, ISATAP and others. The configuration RFCs assume the length in subtler ways, in the link-local addresses, in the EUI-64-based addresses that DHCPv6 may assign and in the collision probabilities that Optimistic Duplicate Address Detection computes.

The document then lists specific failure modes. Methods that derive a multicast group address from a unicast prefix, and the scheme that embeds a rendezvous point address in a multicast address, both assume a longest prefix of 64 bits. The cryptographically generated address format is built on a 64-bit identifier and 64-bit subnet prefix, and 59 bits are used for cryptographic purposes, so more bits for identifiers would strengthen it and longer prefixes would weaken it. NAT64 is fine with a subnet boundary out to /96 but not longer, and prefix translation maps a /64 prefix to another /64 prefix, though the boundary itself could change as long as both sides have the same length. ILNP relies on locally unique 64-bit node identifiers in the identifier field. Secure forms of the multihoming shim protocol depend on cryptographically generated or hash-based addresses, which assume 64 bits. If autoconfiguration were modified to use shorter identifiers, the chance of two hosts picking the same pseudo-random identifier would rise in step, and a /120 prefix would imply an 8-bit identifier with collisions highly probable. The link-local prefix is hard-coded per interface, so hosts using different identifier lengths for link-local addresses would cause confusion.

Tests of current systems show how they behave with other prefix lengths. The autonomous address configuration bit in the prefix information option is honoured only when the prefix length is 64. The on-link bit is honoured for any prefix length, shorter or longer. Nodes that support the route information option accept routes with prefixes of any length. Other observations are more mixed: some forwarding devices work correctly with long prefixes such as /80 or /96, and DHCPv6 is in widespread use with no dependency on the /64 boundary, with deployments of /120 subnets configured by DHCPv6, but there have been definite reports of routers with a performance drop-off or even resource exhaustion for prefixes longer than /64, because some routing chips allocate much less space for longer prefixes to save memory, power and lookup latency, and one type of switch has a content-addressable memory limited to 144 bits, which means the longest prefix usable in a filter there is a /112.

The practical consequence is that a deployment using longer prefixes cannot use autoconfigured addresses and must use manually configured addresses or DHCPv6. One DHCPv6 client unconditionally installs a /64 prefix as on-link when it configures an interface, which is in clear violation of the IPv6 subnet model, motivated by the removal of the on-link assumption. Address management tools treat /64 as the default but let users choose longer prefixes, and all of them would have to be checked in detail. Finally, IPv6 is already deployed at many sites, with staff trained on the existing standards and documentation, tools and middleboxes built on them, which is a large investment that a change would badly disturb.
sections.plainLanguage: Shortening the identifier would ripple through dozens of specifications, many of which state the 64-bit rule outright. It would break particular mechanisms: how multicast group addresses are derived from prefixes, cryptographically generated addresses, and the two forms of translation. It would also make duplicate addresses far more likely, since a /120 subnet leaves only 8 bits of identifier. Tests of current systems show that the automatic address bit in neighbour discovery is only honoured at exactly 64 bits, that some routing chips are built to store long prefixes badly, and that a device with a 144-bit filter memory cannot even hold a /128 address with two ports.

sections.title: Privacy and Scanning
sections.content:
The length of the interface identifier has privacy implications. Where the identifier is meant to be hard to guess, whether or not it is cryptographically generated, more bits are better: with only 20 bits to guess, at most just over a million guesses are needed, which is within the reach of a low-cost attack. How many bits are enough depends on the attacker's resources, but a privacy solution needs to resist an attack requiring billions rather than millions of guesses, and trillions would be better, which suggests at least 40 bits should be available. Subnet prefixes longer than, say, /80 might therefore raise privacy concerns by making the identifier guessable. A prefix long enough to limit addresses to the number of an IPv4 subnet, such as /120, would create the same privacy position as IPv4 except for the absence of NAT, and a host would have to pick a new identifier when it moved to another network to avoid collisions.

The length also affects the defence against scanning attacks. Assuming the attacker knows the prefix length, a longer prefix shrinks the space to scan, to only 256 addresses for a /120. If the attacker does not know the length and assumes /64, routers can trivially discard packets that do not fall inside a real subnet. But an attacker who finds one valid address can scan outwards from it, trying the next address up and down, and will easily find every host in any subnet with a long prefix, because their addresses are close together. Any prefix that contains densely packed valid addresses is therefore vulnerable to a scanning attack without the attacker having to guess the prefix length at all. To preserve IPv6's advantage over IPv4 in resisting such attacks, the prefix must be short enough to allow sparse allocation of identifiers within each subnet, which again points to prefixes longer than about /80 being undesirable. That is exactly the converse of the argument for longer prefixes to resist a neighbour discovery cache attack. The document notes that other resource exhaustion attacks of a similar kind might exist, and that the analysis assumes a conventional deployment with many end systems in one broadcast domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The shorter the identifier, the easier it is to guess, and a privacy scheme has to survive an attack that tries billions of values, which needs at least 40 bits. Long prefixes also make a network easier to scan: an attacker who finds one address can work outwards from it and find the rest. Both arguments point the same way, towards keeping the prefix short enough that the addresses inside it are spread out.

items.title: Multicast group addresses
items.text: Deriving a group address from a unicast prefix assumes a longest prefix of 64 bits.

items.title: Cryptographic addresses
items.text: The format is built on a 64-bit identifier, with 59 bits used for cryptographic purposes.

items.title: NAT64
items.text: Flexible down to a /96 boundary, but not beyond it.

items.title: Prefix translation
items.text: Maps one /64 prefix to another, though both sides could share a different length.

items.title: ILNP
items.text: Relies on locally unique 64-bit node identifiers in the identifier field.

items.title: Secure multihoming
items.text: Depends on cryptographic or hash-based addresses, which assume 64 bits.

items.title: Duplicate addresses
items.text: A /120 prefix leaves an 8-bit identifier, and collisions would be highly probable.

items.title: Link-local addresses
